contributions.headingText: Cemento-osseous dysplasia (COD) is a non-neoplastic fibro-osseous lesion arising only in the tooth-bearing areas of the jaws.

DA07.3 Disturbances in tooth formation & Florid cemento-osseous dysplasia

2E83.1 Benign osteogenic tumours of bone or articular cartilage of lower jaw & Periapical cemento-osseous dysplasia of lower jaw
Not recommended: osseous dysplasia; cemental dysplasia; cementoma.
Periapical cemento-osseous dysplasia (PCOD); focal cemento-osseous dysplasia (FocCOD); florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (FCOD); familial florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (FFCOD)

PCOD predominantly involves the periapical bone of the anterior mandibular teeth; FocCOD involves a single, usually posterior, mandibular tooth; and FCOD involves multiple tooth-bearing quadrants {32565263; 29267533}. FFCOD almost always has the same distribution as FCOD {32315206}.

CODs are usually asymptomatic, non-expansile lesions associated with the roots of vital teeth. Some cases of FocCOD and as many as 25% of FCOD cases may expand the jaw, either directly or after cyst formation, sometimes markedly {27161103}. Patients with FocCOD, FCOD, and FFCOD are prone to developing osteomyelitis in their late sclerotic stage, with pain and discharge {27161103; 27422424}. COD may remain in edentulous jaw after tooth extraction. FFCOD has an earlier age of onset than FCOD, often affecting tooth eruption, and is prone to marked expansion, usually in the anterior mandible but sometimes multifocally {32315206}, leading to confusion with familial gigantiform cementoma.

Imaging

Radiographic features are characteristic and often diagnostic. The early stage of all subtypes of COD produces well-defined periapical radiolucencies continuous with periodontal ligament, enlarging slowly before developing internal, usually central, radiopacities and patchy sclerosis beyond a well-defined radiolucent rim. Later, lesions become radiodense with lobulated dense mineralization {32565263; 29267533}. FocCOD is more variable {9394387}.

COD is the most common benign fibro-osseous lesion of the jaws, with a strong predilection for middle-aged women {25409854; 33878496}, most commonly African and African-American women, but with a significant incidence in Asian women {24326826} and White women {32565263}. FFCOD has a less marked racial and sex predilection {32315206}.

The pathogenesis is unknown for PCOD, FocCOD, and FCOD. The members of one family with FFCOD have been shown to carry a mutation in ANO5 that is proposed to destabilize this transmembrane ion channel {30996299}. The mutated locus is distinct from that in gnathodiaphysial dysplasia, in which there are multiple cemento-ossifying fibromas {27068316}.
Multiple variably sized, gritty fragments of haemorrhagic bone and soft tissue

All COD subtypes exhibit identical microscopic features dependent on the degree of maturation. There are varying proportions of osteoid and woven bone; mature lamellar bone; and rounded, densely basophilic, cementum-like mineralizations; these appear in a cellular fibrous connective tissue stroma of loosely arranged collagen and prominently dilated, thin-walled vessels. Osteoblastic rimming is rare. There is often focal high cellularity. Maturing lesions show increasing calcification with often prominent reversal lines and reduced vascularity. Late-stage lesions are characterized by the coalescence of calcified tissue that forms hypocellular, sclerotic masses with limited stroma {9377196; 30887390; 32565263; 33878496}.

Differential diagnosis

Approximately 10% of cases may develop expansile cystic degeneration resembling solitary bone cyst {21683027}, usually in the mandible in late-stage disease. Expansile areas in FFCOD may be difficult to distinguish from cemento-ossifying fibroma {32315206} if the background disease is not appreciated.
Essential: radiological features are almost always diagnostic; benign fibro-osseous lesion histologically.

Radiological diagnosis is usual, with periodic follow-up for expansion, cyst formation, and osteomyelitis. Surgical intervention is indicated exclusively for symptomatic cases {32565263; 27422424}, because osteomyelitis is a common complication of biopsy or tooth extraction. Cysts may recur after surgery.
